records.anchor_quote: What is the average distance from the origin to a point on the polar curve
records.description: The part asks for the average distance from the origin to points on the same polar curve over the stated angle interval. The distance from the origin is the radial function itself, so the average value of that function over the angle interval is what must be formed and evaluated.
diagnostic_distinctions: radius squared in the integrand: the polar area formula is imported where average value was asked
averaging factor omitted: average value and total accumulation confused
indefinite integral presented: definite integral notation is not controlled
records.difficulty_notes: Two concepts joined, average value transported into a polar setting, calculator workflow, high notation risk because the area integral of the same curve squares the radius.
records.name: 2019 BC Q2(b): average distance from the origin to a point on a polar curve
records.notation_requirements: Average value written as one over the angle span times the integral of the radial function.
records.notes: archetype_gap resolved: the average value of a radial function preserves the invariant structure of BC-QA-08001, so it is recorded as the variant BC-QV-08001-04 rather than as a new archetype (sg-19:3).
scoring_behaviors: The scoring guidelines for this year number the points within each part, such as the first point and the second point of the part, rather than running from P1 to P9 across the whole question (sg-19:3).
Integral point: the integral of the radial function, not its square, over the stated angles earns it; the averaging factor is not part of this point (samples-19-q2:9).
Answer point: the average distance correct to three decimals earns it; an indefinite integral in place of a definite one earns nothing (samples-19-q2:11).
